title: Genesis 24. The Cup of the Well.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 24. The Cup of the Well.
Abraham was old, well advanced in days.
The Lord had blessed Abraham in all things.
The man who left Ur with nothing now has everything.
Flocks, herds, silver, gold, servants, camels, donkeys.
The man who was a stranger in Canaan owns a burial plot and the son of the promise.
But the son has no wife.
The Cup that was planted in Sarah's grave has not yet produced the next vessel.
Abraham speaks to his servant, the oldest of his house,
who ruled over all he had.
Put your hand under my thigh.
I will make you swear by the Lord,
the God of heaven and the God of the earth,
that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I live.
But you shall go to my country and to my kindred,
and take a wife for my son Isaac.
The oath is placed under the thigh,
the same place where the covenant of circumcision was written.
The sign of the covenant is the sign of the oath.
The wife for Isaac must not come from the people of the land.
She must come from the kindred.
The Cup that was promised to bless all nations is not yet ready to marry into them.
First, it must be kept within the line.
The servant asks:
What if the woman is not willing to follow me to this land?
Must I bring your son back to the land you came from?
Abraham says:
See to it that you do not bring my son back there.
The Lord, the God of heaven,
who took me from my father's house and from the land of my birth,
who spoke to me and swore to me, saying,
To your offspring I will give this land,
He will send His angel before you.
And you shall take a wife for my son from there.
If the woman is not willing to follow you,
then you shall be free from this oath.
Only do not bring my son back there.
The command is absolute: do not bring Isaac back.
The Cup that was carried out of Ur must not return to Ur.
The promise that was given in a land Abraham did not yet own must not go back to the land he left.
What God brought out, man must not take back.
The servant can go.
Isaac cannot.
The servant puts his hand under Abraham's thigh and swears.
He takes ten camels,
departs with all kinds of good things from his master,
and goes to Mesopotamia, to the city of Nahor.
He makes the camels kneel outside the city by the well of water at the time of evening,
the time when women go out to draw water.
A well.
Evening.
Women drawing water.
The same elements that appeared in Hagar's wilderness, a spring, a woman,
the Angel of the Lord.
The same elements that appeared at Beersheba, a well, an oath,
a tamarisk tree.
The Cup is always found near water.
The promise always meets its vessel at a well.
The servant prays: Lord, God of my master Abraham,
please grant me success today and show steadfast love to my master Abraham.
I am standing by the spring of water.
The daughters of the men of the city are coming out to draw water.
Let it happen that the young woman to whom I say:
Please let down your jar that I may drink, and she answers:
Drink, and I will give your camels drink also,
let her be the one You have appointed for Your servant Isaac.
By this I shall know that You have shown steadfast love to my master.
The servant sets a test.
But the test is not for God.
It is for the servant's own eyes,
a sign so specific that its fulfillment cannot be coincidence.
A woman who offers water to a stranger is ordinary.
A woman who offers water to ten camels is extraordinary.
A camel can drink twenty to thirty gallons of water after a journey.
Ten camels.
That is two hundred to three hundred gallons drawn by hand from a well,
one jar at a time, carried up the steps,
poured into a trough, again and again until they finish.
The woman who passes this test does not merely offer hospitality.
She offers labor.
Exhaustion.
Hours of drawing water for strangers' animals.
The Cup of the covenant is looking for a vessel that gives beyond what is asked.
Before he had finished speaking, Rebekah came out.
Born to Bethuel the son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor,
Abraham's brother.
With her jar on her shoulder.
The young woman was very beautiful to look at.
A virgin.
No man had known her.
She went down to the spring, filled her jar, and came up.
Before he finished speaking.
The prayer was answered in the middle of the sentence.
The same God who said I will surely return to you about this time next year answers a prayer before it is finished.
The Cup does not wait for the vessel to complete its petition.
The vessel is already on her way.
The servant runs to meet her.
Please give me a drink, a little water from your jar.
She says: Drink, my lord.
She hurries, lets down her jar upon her hand,
and gives him drink.
When she has finished giving him drink, she says:
I will also draw for your camels, until they have finished drinking.
She hurries and empties her jar into the trough and runs again to the well to draw,
and draws for all his camels.
She runs.
The same word used for Abraham running to the three visitors in chapter eighteen.
The same urgency.
The same generosity.
Rebekah does not walk to the well.
She runs.
She draws.
She pours.
She runs again.
For ten camels.
For a stranger.
For a servant she has never met.
The Cup of the covenant is looking for a woman who gives more than she is asked,
and Rebekah gives until the camels finish.
The man gazes at her in silence,
waiting to learn whether the Lord had made his journey prosperous or not.
When the camels finish drinking,
the man takes a gold ring of half a shekel weight and two bracelets weighing ten shekels of gold,
and says: Whose daughter are you?
Please tell me.
Is there room in your father's house for us to lodge?
She says: I am the daughter of Bethuel, the son of Milcah,
whom she bore to Nahor.
We have straw and feed enough, and room to lodge.
The daughter of Bethuel.
The granddaughter of Nahor, Abraham's brother.
The woman named at the end of chapter twenty-two, Rebekah,
appears at the well.
The Cup that was tested on Moriah and buried at Machpelah now stands at a well in Aram,
wearing gold given by a servant who has not yet told her who he is or why he came.
The man bows his head and worships the Lord.
Blessed be the Lord, the God of my master Abraham,
who has not forsaken His steadfast love and faithfulness toward my master.
As for me,
the Lord has led me on the way to the house of my master's kinsmen.
The servant worships before the girl's family is consulted.
Before the negotiation.
Before the gifts.
Before the meal.
He worships because the answer came before the prayer was finished.
The Cup was already full.
The vessel was already there.
Rebekah runs and tells her mother's house.
Her brother Laban sees the ring and the bracelets and hears her words,
and runs to the man at the spring.
He says: Come in, you blessed of the Lord.
Why do you stand outside?
I have prepared the house and room for the camels.
Laban sees the gold before he hears the story.
The same Laban who will later deceive Jacob with his daughters is introduced here as a man who responds to wealth.
But the servant will not eat until he has told his message.
He tells everything.
Abraham's wealth.
Isaac's birth.
The oath.
The journey.
The prayer at the well.
The sign.
Rebekah's answer.
The gold.
The camels.
The running.
The drawing.
Every detail, told in full,
in the hearing of Laban and Bethuel and everyone in the house.
Then he says: Now,
if you will deal kindly and truly with my master, tell me.
If not, tell me,
that I may turn to the right or to the left.
Laban and Bethuel answer: The thing comes from the Lord.
We cannot speak to you bad or good.
Behold, Rebekah is before you.
Take her and go.
Let her be the wife of your master's son,
as the Lord has spoken.
The thing comes from the Lord.
The family that does not carry the covenant recognizes the covenant's God.
The same words the Hittites used,
you are a prince of God among us, are echoed here:
the thing comes from the Lord.
The Cup is recognized by the people who did not receive it.
The servant brings out jewelry of silver and gold and clothing,
and gives them to Rebekah.
He gives precious things to her brother and mother.
They eat and drink and stay the night.
In the morning, he says: Send me away to my master.
Her brother and mother say:
Let the young woman stay with us a few days,
at least ten.
After that she shall go.
He says: Do not hinder me.
Since the Lord has prospered my way, send me away,
that I may go to my master.
They say: We will call the young woman and ask her.
They called Rebekah and said: Will you go with this man?
She said: I will go.
Three words.
I will go.
The woman who drew water for ten camels,
who received gold from a stranger,
who heard a story about a God she was not raised to worship,
who has never seen the man she is going to marry, says:
I will go.
The same voluntariness that was absent from every arranged marriage in Genesis so far.
Sarah was taken by Pharaoh.
Sarah was taken by Abimelech.
Hagar was given.
Rebekah is asked.
And she chooses.
They bless Rebekah: Our sister,
may you be the mother of thousands of ten thousands,
and may your offspring possess the gate of those who hate him.
The blessing echoes the oath God swore to Abraham on Moriah:
your offspring shall possess the gate of his enemies.
The family that sends Rebekah away speaks the promise over her without knowing they are speaking it.
The Cup that was given to Abraham is now spoken by Nahor's household over Nahor's granddaughter.
Rebekah arose, with her young women.
They rode on the camels and followed the man.
The servant took Rebekah and went his way.
Isaac came from the way of Beer-lahai-roi,
the well of the Living One who sees me.
The well Hagar named in chapter sixteen when God found her in the wilderness.
Isaac is living near the place where Ishmael's mother named God El Roi.
The son of the promise dwells near the well of the woman who was cast out.
Isaac went out to meditate in the field toward evening.
He lifted up his eyes and saw, and behold, camels were coming.
Rebekah lifted up her eyes.
She saw Isaac.
She dismounted from the camel.
She said to the servant:
Who is that man walking in the field to meet us?
The servant said: It is my master.
She took her veil and covered herself.
The same gesture as Shem and Japheth, covering.
But where they covered their father's nakedness backward,
Rebekah covers her own face forward.
The woman who drew water openly at the well now veils herself before the man she has come to marry.
The Cup that was drawn in public is now hidden in private.
The vessel covers itself before the one it is given to.
The servant told Isaac all the things he had done.
Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother.
He took Rebekah, and she became his wife.
He loved her.
And Isaac was comforted after his mother's death.
Sarah's tent.
The tent that was empty since chapter twenty-three.
The tent where Sarah laughed behind the flap.
The tent where the three visitors asked: Where is Sarah, your wife?
The tent where the promise was spoken and the promise was doubted,
and the promise was fulfilled.
That tent now holds Rebekah.
The Cup that was buried in a cave is opened again.
Not by retrieving Sarah.
By bringing Rebekah into the tent.
The covenant continues through a woman who drew water and gave drink and said I will go and covered herself and entered a tent where another woman once laughed.
Isaac was comforted.
The son who nearly died on Moriah,
who walked up the mountain carrying wood and came through the test alive,
now receives comfort from a woman who came from the same family his father left.
The promise does not go back to Ur.
The woman comes forward from Ur's kindred.
The Cup does not return to the place it was poured.
The vessel comes to the place where the Cup is kept.
And the man who was the offering on the mountain is now the husband in the tent.
The promise holds.
The well holds.
The woman holds.
The tent holds.
